Machine learning research has rapidly transformed defensive detection systems, but its potential in offensive tooling remains largely untapped. Dan Petro and Ben Morris introduce DeepHack, an open-source autonomous penetration testing agent that utilizes neural networks and reinforcement learning algorithms to discover and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications without requiring pre-programmed attack signatures or prior knowledge of target application architectures.

Architecture and Reinforcement Learning Pipeline

DeepHack operates through an iterative trial-and-error feedback loop, observing application HTTP responses and rewarding successful state transitions that lead toward database extraction, authentication bypass, or command execution. Petro and Morris explain the neural network architecture, reward functions, and vector representations used to model web inputs, demonstrating how a single generalized learning algorithm adapts to attack multiple vulnerability classes such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.

Autonomous Exploitation in Practice

The authors demonstrate DeepHack operating in real-time against benchmark vulnerable applications. Without human intervention or static wordlists, the agent systematically probes input fields, infers backend database syntax from error responses, and autonomously optimizes exploitation payloads to retrieve restricted data, illustrating how machine learning agents can dramatically outpace human penetration testers in repetitive payload mutation.

The Future of Offensive Artificial Intelligence

The presentation explores the broader implications of weaponized machine learning in offensive cybersecurity operations. Petro and Morris project the trajectory of autonomous exploitation frameworks, discussing how future iterations will incorporate natural language processing to navigate complex application logic and automate lateral movement. They warn that organizations must prepare defenses against automated, adaptive cyber attacks that evolve faster than manual incident response procedures can mitigate.

talks.title: If You Give a Mouse a Microchip
talks.teaser: Demonstrates modifying ARM Cortex-M mouse firmware to covertly stage and deliver arbitrary payloads through standard USB HID interfaces in high-security tournament settings.
talks.summary:
Physical Peripherals in High Stakes Environments

Competitive esports tournaments feature multi-million dollar prize pools where the incentive to cheat has driven players to develop sophisticated evasion techniques. Because event organizers enforce strict controls on target tournament PCs—including disabling internet access and locking down USB mass storage—players are still permitted to bring their own competition-grade mice and keyboards, creating an overlooked physical attack vector.

Exploiting ARM Cortex M Gaming Peripherals

Modern commercial gaming mice frequently feature onboard ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers and internal flash memory to store custom DPI settings, macro bindings, and user profile configurations across different computers. Mark Williams and Rob Stanley demonstrate how an attacker can reverse engineer the peripheral's firmware and embed a malicious payload delivery routine into unused sectors of the onboard flash memory without disrupting standard optical tracking or button inputs.

Payload Staging Over USB Human Interface Devices

Because the modified mouse continues to operate as an expected Human Interface Device (HID), it bypasses perimeter controls and operating system USB mass storage restrictions. Upon receiving a covert physical trigger sequence or timer condition, the compromised firmware initiates a rapid burst of synthetic keystroke events, opening hidden execution contexts to stage and launch compiled game cheats or arbitrary executables directly into system memory.

Detection Tradeoffs and Hardware Defenses

The authors evaluate the practical tradeoffs of peripheral-based HID attacks, noting that automated window spawning and keystroke injection remain observable to attentive observers or local audit logging agents. They discuss countermeasures for tournament organizers and high-security enterprise facilities, including mandatory hardware quarantine policies, firmware signature verification, and the adoption of USB device whitelisting tools that restrict non-standard HID descriptors.

talks.title: I Know What You Are by the Smell of Your Wifi
talks.teaser: Extracts granular device models and hardware revisions by passive fingerprinting of 802.11 Wi-Fi management frames and probe request signatures.
talks.summary:
Limitations of Traditional Network Device Fingerprinting

Network administrators and security analysts commonly rely on passive fingerprinting techniques to catalog connected client devices, inspecting DHCP options, HTTP User-Agent strings, and mDNS or SSDP broadcast announcements. Denton Gentry explains that these traditional network-layer indicators provide only coarse identification—frequently distinguishing merely between generic operating system categories while failing to differentiate specific hardware revisions or device generations.

Extracting Signatures from 802.11 Management Frames

By shifting inspection down to the 802.11 wireless physical and data link layers, analysts can examine the precise structural composition of unencrypted Wi-Fi management frames. Gentry demonstrates that probe request frames contain distinct Information Elements (IEs)—including supported data rates, extended capabilities, vendor-specific tags, and HT/VHT capabilities—that reflect the specific Wi-Fi chipset and driver implementation integrated into a device.

Granular Hardware Model Identification

The talk illustrates how subtle variations in the ordering and parameters of Information Elements allow passive listeners to distinguish between closely related hardware models. Using real-world capture datasets, Gentry demonstrates differentiating an iPhone 5 from an iPhone 5S, or distinguishing specific Samsung Galaxy and LG mobile revisions simply by analyzing the distinctive "smell" of their wireless probe requests before any association or network connection occurs.

Security and Operational Applications

Passive wireless fingerprinting provides network defenders and security researchers with non-intrusive asset discovery capabilities, enabling automated inventory of mobile hardware entering monitored facilities. Gentry outlines the practical implementation of signature matching engines and discusses the operational implications for client tracking, network access control, and privacy defense against physical location surveillance.
